==English== {{wp}} ===Alternative forms=== * {{alt|en|dike||US}} ===Etymology 1=== {{root|en|ine-pro|*dʰeygʷ-}} A variant of {{m|en|dike}}, from {{der|en|enm-nor|dik}} and {{m|enm|dike||[[ditch]]}}, from {{der|en|non|díki||[[ditch]]}}. Influenced by {{der|en|dum|dijc||[[ditch]]; [[dam]]}} and {{der|en|gml|dīk||[[dam]]}}.''Oxford Dictionaries''. "[https://web.archive.org/web/20160403071221/http://www.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/english/dyke dyke]". ''See also'' '''[[ditch]]'''. Ultimately from {{der|en|gem-pro|*dīkiją||trench, ditch}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*dʰeygʷ-||stick into, pierce; dig, stick a spade into}}. The semantic evolution (also seen in several cognate words) was from "stick (a spade) into" to "dig" to "hole or other product of digging", "excavation", then the ridge of earth created when excavating a ditch, then to a ridge of earth intended to prevent flooding.{{R:Etymonline}} ====Pronunciation==== * {{IPA|en|/ˈdaɪ̯k/}} ** {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Vealhurl-dyke.wav|a=Southern England}} ** {{IPA|en|/ˈdʌɪ̯k/|/ˈdɜɪ̯k/|a=Canadian raising}} * {{IPA|en|/ˈdʌi̯k/|/ˈdəi̯k/|a=Scottish}} * {{rhymes|en|aɪk|s=1}} ====Noun==== {{en-noun}} {{tlb|en|British spelling}} # An [[earthwork]] [[raise]]d to [[prevent]] [[inundation]] of [[low]] [[land]] by the [[sea]] or [[flood]]ing [[river]]s. #* {{quote-book|en|year=1891|author=Susan Hale|title=The Story of Nations: Mexico|page=100 |passage=The king of Texcuco advised the building of a great '''dike''', so thick and strong as to keep out the water.}} # {{lb|en|now|chiefly|Scotland}} A [[low]] [[embankment]] or [[stone]] [[wall]] [[serving]] as an [[enclosure]] and [[boundary]] [[marker]]. #* {{quote-book|en|date=2023-02-21|author=Nick Aitken|title=Dry Stone Walling - Materials and Techniques|publisher=The Crowood Press|isbn=9780719841682 |text=The Galloway Dyke / In southwest Scotland there is a local style of dry stone '''dyke''' that is now recognized as 'the Galloway '''dyke'''', although when this pattern of {{SIC}} was first developed, it was simply described as 'the sheep '''dyke''''.'}} # A [[raise]]d [[causeway]]. # {{lb|en|historical}} A [[long]], [[narrow]] [[hollow]] [[dug]] from the [[ground]] to [[conduct]] [[water]]. # {{lb|en|dialect}} [[any|Any]] [[navigable]] [[watercourse]]. # {{lb|en|dialect}} [[any|Any]] [[watercourse]]. # {{lb|en|dialect}} [[any|Any]] [[small]] [[body]] of [[water]]. # {{lb|en|geology}} A [[body]] of [[rock]] ([[usually]] [[igneous]]) [[originally]] [[fill]]ing a [[fissure]] but [[now]] [[often]] [[rising]] above the [[older]] [[stratum]] as [[it]] is [[erode]]d away. # {{lb|en|now|chiefly|Australia|slang}} A [[place]] to [[urinate]] and [[defecate]]: an [[outhouse]] or [[lavatory]]. #* {{quote-book|en|year=1977|author=Ian Slack-Smith|chapter=The Passing of the Twin Seater|title=The Cubbaroo Tales |passage=In Cubbaroo's dim distant past
They built a double [[dyke]].
Back to back in the yard it stood
An architectural dream in wood.}} # An [[embankment]] [[form]]ed by the [[spoil]] from the [[creation]] of a [[ditch]]. # {{lb|en|obsolete}} [[any|Any]] [[hollow]] [[dug]] into the [[ground]]. # {{lb|en|historical}} A [[long]], [[narrow]] [[hollow]] [[dug]] from the [[ground]] to [[serve]] as a [[boundary]] [[marker]]. # A [[wall]], especially {{lb|en|obsolete|outside|heraldry}} a masoned [[city]] or castle [[wall]]. #* {{quote-book|en|year=1722|author=Alexander Nisbet|title=A System of Heraldry Speculative and Practical|page=82 |text=''Inchbrakie'' gives for Arms, Or, ''a '''Dyke''' (or Wall) Feſsways, broke down in ſome places, and in Baſe a Roſe'' Gules, ''on a chief'' Sable ''three Eſcalops of the'' firſt. The ''Dyke (or Wall)'' here, is aſſumed not only to difference, but to perpetuate the valiant Action of ''Graham'' before mentioned; in throwing down the Wall and Ditch, which the ''Romans'' made betwixt ''Forth'' and ''Clyde'', to keep out the ''Scots'', [...]}} #* {{quote-book|en|year=1894|author=Henry Gough; James Parker|title=A Glossary of Terms Used in Heraldry|page=608 |text=''Wall'', (sometimes called a ''dyke, fr. ''mur'') : this is generally found in connection with ''castles'' or ''towns'' which are ''walled'' (''muraillé''). A wall of which kind should be masoned (fr. ''maçonné'') and embattled (fr. ''crenellé''), even though this be not specified. [...] Or, a '''dyke''' [or wall] fesswise [masoned proper] broken down in some places gules; [...] —G{{smallcaps|raham}}, Inchbrakie, Scotland [similar arms borne by G{{smallcaps|ræme}} of Stapleton].}} #* {{quote-book|en|date=2023-02-21|author=Nick Aitken|title=Dry Stone Walling - Materials and Techniques|publisher=The Crowood Press|isbn=9780719841682 |text=The Galloway Dyke / In southwest Scotland there is a local style of dry stone '''dyke''' that is now recognized as 'the Galloway '''dyke'''', although when this pattern of was first developed, it was simply described as 'the sheep '''dyke''''.'}} # {{lb|en|dialect|mining}} A [[fissure]] in a [[rock]] [[stratum]] [[fill]]ed with [[intrusive]] [[rock]]; a [[fault]]. =====Synonyms===== * {{sense|long, narrow excavation}} {{l|en|ditch}}, {{l|en|trench}}, {{l|en|fosse}} * {{sense|small body of water}} {{l|en|puddle}}, {{l|en|pond}}, {{l|en|pool}}, {{l|en|lakelet}}, {{l|en|mere}} * {{sense|any hollow}} {{l|en|den}}, {{l|en|cave}}, {{l|en|hole}}, {{l|en|pit}} * {{sense|any embankment}} {{l|en|bank}}, {{l|en|embankment}}, {{l|en|earthwork}} * {{sense|barrier of stone or earth}} {{l|en|bank}}, {{l|en|embankment}}, {{l|en|dam}}, {{l|en|levee}}, {{l|en|breakwater}}, {{l|en|floodwall}}, {{l|en|seawall}} =====Derived terms===== {{col3|en|Devil's Dyke|dykelet |dry-stone dyke |dyke-back |dyke bottom |dyke phase|dyke-phase |dyke road |dyke-rock |dyke swarm|dyke-swarm |fail dyke |February fill-dyke|fill-dyke |finger in the dyke |King's Dyke |dyke up}} =====Related terms===== * {{l|en|ditch}} * {{l|en|dig}} =====Translations===== {{trans-see|ditch}} {{trans-top|ditch and bank running alongside each other}} * Bulgarian: * Dutch: * Finnish: * French: * German: * Italian: * Polish: * Portuguese: * Russian: {{t|ru|сто́чная кана́ва|f}}, {{t+|ru|кана́ва|f}}, {{t+|ru|ров|m}}, {{t+|ru|транше́я|f}} {{trans-bottom}} {{trans-top|barrier to prevent flooding}} * Armenian: * Bulgarian: * Catalan: * Czech: * Danish: * Dutch: * Esperanto: * Estonian: * Finnish: * French: * Georgian: * German: * Greek: * Hindi: * Irish: * Italian: * Japanese: * Korean: * Latin: * Latvian: * Macedonian: * Māori: * Plautdietsch: * Polish: * Portuguese: * Romanian: * Russian: {{t+|ru|да́мба}} * Spanish: * Turkish: * Vietnamese: * Welsh: {{trans-bottom}} {{trans-top|geology: body of once igneous rock injected into older rocks}} * Arabic: * Finnish: * German: * Hungarian: * Irish: * Italian: * Polish: * Spanish: * Swedish: * Turkish: {{trans-bottom}} ====Verb==== {{en-verb}} # {{label|en|transitive|_|or|_|intransitive}} To [[dig]], ''[[particularly]]'' to [[create]] a [[ditch]]. #* {{RQ:Kingsley Hereward the Wake|volume=I|page=4|passage=He finds out, soon enough for his weal and his bane, that he is stronger than Nature: and right tyrannously and irreverently he lords it over her, clearing, delving, '''dyking''', building, without fear or shame.}} # {{label|en|transitive}} To [[scour]] a [[watercourse]]. # {{label|en|transitive}} To [[steep]] (fibers) within a [[watercourse]]. ===Etymology 2=== {{wp|+ (slang)}} {{unc|en}}. Attested since the 1940s (in Berrey and Van den Bark’s 1942 ''American Thesaurus of Slang'')"dike, dyke, n.3" ''The Oxford English Dictionary''. 2nd ed. 1989, OED Online, Oxford UP, April 4, 2000.[http://dictionary.oed.com/cgi/entry/50064031]. or 30s.{{R:MWO}} Semantic development from {{m|en|dyke||ditch}} has been proposed, and some sources from the 1890s are said to record ''dyke'' as slang for "vulva" and ''hedge of the dyke'' as slang for "pubic hair",{{R:GDoS|id=djbkqki|entry=hedge}} but ''Green's Dictionary of Slang'' says this is not found in connection to lesbianism and Dictionary.com considers a connection unlikely. {{m|en|bull dyke|Bull dyke}} / {{m|en|bulldike}} is attested earlier, in reference to women since at least the 1920s{{R:Dictionary.com|bulldyke}}{{R:Etymonline}} (the 29 July 1892 ''Decatur Daily Review'' in [[Illinois]] mentions a woman who "won the affections of Harvey Neal, alias 'Bulldyke'", whose gender is unclear);{{R:GDoS|id=x3tzlsa|entry=bull-dyke}}{{cite-web |title=Word Origins: dyke |url=http://www.wordorigins.org/index.php/more/273/ |accessdate=3 December 2019 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20191203192616/http://www.wordorigins.org/index.php/more/273/ |archivedate=3 December 2019 }} compare {{m|en|dike||''noun:'' well-dressed man; ''verb:'' be well dressed}}), {{m|en|bulldyker}}, and {{m|en|bulldyking}}, which are all attested earlier than bare ''dyke'', e.g. in Parke's 1906 ''Human Sexuality'', in the speech of Philadelphians,Joseph Richardson Parke, ''Human Sexuality: A Medico-literary Treatise'' (1906), page 309: "In American homosexual argot, female inverts, or lesbian lovers, are known euphemistically as 'bulldykers,' whatever that may mean: at least that is their sobriquet in the 'Red Light' district of Philadelphia. and backcountry black Americans. Compare {{m|en|bulldagger}}, attested since around the same time and used especially by black women.JoAnne Myers, ''Historical Dictionary of the Lesbian and Gay Liberation Movements'' (2013), p. 97Yetta Howard, ''Ugly Differences: Queer Female Sexuality in the Underground'' (2018), p. 238, which also refers to "Bogus, “The 'Queen B,'” and Walker, “The Debutante in Harlem,” 58–102, and “Lesbian Pulp in Black and White,” 103–138, for considerations of the figure of the black bulldagger in other Harlem Renaissance texts." Other linguists suggested that ''bull dyke(r)'' referred to strong black women who dug dikes, or derived from {{m|en|bull}} + {{m|en|dick}}, perhaps in reference to black men.Charles Panati, ''Sexy Origins and Intimate Things'' (1998), p. 181: "In fact, “bulldiking” is one of the earliest phrases in which the term “dike" has tough female overtones. It appeared in the American South in the nineteenth century, used by black Americans. Some linguists believe that strong black women who helped dig watercourses on Southern plantations were called “bulldikes.” Others, however, claim that "dike" is really a corruption of "dick", slang for "penis," and [...] argue that in the American South, black men who worked on plantations were called "bull dicks" by their white owners." It has also been suggested ''dyke'' is a shortening of {{m|en|morphodyke}}, from ''[[morphodite]]'', from ''[[hermaphrodite]]'',{{cite-book|en|year=1991|author=Sterling K. Eisiminger|title=The Consequence of Error and Other Language Essays|publisher=Peter Lang Pub Incorporated|text=Archibald Hill suggests that both dike and dyke are respectively clipped forms of morphodite and morphodyke, themselves clipped and mispronounced forms of hermaphrodite (A.S. 57.1).}} but the derivation may go in the other direction instead, with ''morphodyke'' being a blend of ''morphodite'' with the already-extant word ''dyke''. ====Noun==== {{en-noun}} {{tlb|en|slang|vulgar|usually|derogatory|and|offensive}} # {{sid|en|lesbian}} {{lb|en|anti-LGBTQ slur}} A [[lesbian]], particularly one with [[masculine]] or [[butch]] [[trait]]s or [[behavior]]; {{qualifier|by extension}} a [[non-heterosexual]] woman. #: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:female homosexual}} #: {{cot|en|faggot}} # A [[masculine]] woman. =====Usage notes===== * This term for a lesbian is often derogatory (or taken as such) when used by straight people but is also used by some lesbians and bisexual women to refer to themselves positively; see {{w|reclaimed word}} and {{w|reappropriation}}. =====Derived terms===== {{col|en |bi-dyke |big dyke energy |boydyke |bull dyke |busy as a dyke in a hardware store |designer dyke |diesel dyke |dykedar |dykedom |dykehood |dykeling |dyke out |dykephobia |dykery |dyke tyke |dykey |dykish |dykon |kike dyke |leatherdyke |tryke }} =====Translations===== {{trans-top-also|masculine lesbian|butch|lesbian}} * Akan: * Danish: * Finnish: * French: * German: * Japanese: * Polish: * Portuguese: * Russian: {{t+|ru|кобёл|m}} {{trans-bottom}} {{checktrans-top}} * Danish: {{t|da|lebbe|c}} * Dutch: {{t+|nl|pot|f}} * French: {{t+|fr|gouine|f}} * German: {{t+|de|Lesbe|f}} * Italian: {{t+|it|lesbica|f}} * Polish: {{t+|pl|lesba|f}} * Russian: {{t+|ru|лесбия́нка|f}}, {{t+|ru|ле́сби|f}} * Serbo-Croatian: {{t+|sh|lezbijka|f}} * Spanish: {{t+|es|tortillera|f}}, {{t+|es|bollo|f}} * Swedish: {{t+|sv|flata|c}} * Tagalog: {{t|tl|tibo}} * Turkish: {{t+|tr|sevici}}, {{t+|tr|ablacı|q=slang}} {{trans-bottom}} ===References=== {{reflist}} * ''Oxford English Dictionary'', "dike | dyke, ''n.¹''" & "dike | dyke, ''v.¹''". ===Derived terms=== {{col|en|babydyke|byke}} ===Anagrams=== * {{anagrams|en|a=deky|E.D.
